valuation_philosophy: Marlin Global is an NZX-listed, closed-end investment company (LIC) managed externally by Fisher Funds, not an operating business: it holds a ~NZ$210-220m diversified portfolio of ~26-29 international growth equities (Microsoft, Amazon, Meta, Mastercard, Tencent, Nvidia, etc.), has no employees, no revenue in the operating sense, no capex, no working-capital cycle, and no stock-based compensation. A standard FCF/WACC DCF is inapplicable: reported OperatingCashFlow is a portfolio-turnover artefact and NetIncome/EPS is dominated by unrealised/realised mark-to-market portfolio swings (FY2021 +$69.2m, FY2022 -$60.4m on the same order of magnitude of shares) rather than an operating trend. This model instead uses the NAV-compounding + exit-discount framework applied consistently to the other LIC names in this research folder (AFI.NZ, BIT.NZ, FIH.U, FRFHF): (1) project NAV per share forward using a total-return assumption (long-run global growth-equity return net of Marlin's demonstrated multi-year benchmark underperformance and its ~1.25%-1.5% fee drag) split between per-share NAV growth and the formulaic 2%-of-average-NAV-per-quarter (~8%/yr) distribution -- because that payout formula persistently exceeds underlying NAV growth, Marlin's NAV per share has been essentially FLAT to mildly negative over 8 years ($0.89 FY2017 to $0.95 FY2025, +0.82%/yr) despite a 7.3% p.a. 5-year Adjusted NAV Return, confirming total return is delivered almost entirely via distributions, not NAV compounding; (2) apply a scenario exit discount/premium to NAV, since the market-clearing valuation metric for a closed-end LIC is its price/NAV discount, not an earnings multiple -- Marlin's own history spans a 30.5% PREMIUM (FY2021, COVID-era growth bubble) to a ~16% discount (Aug-2026, the most recent print); (3) headline intrinsic value = today's NAV per share x (1 + scenario fair discount); (4) a separate 5-year IRR build (PV of interim dividends + PV of year-5 exit value at cost of equity) is shown as a cross-check/memo capturing NAV compounding over the horizon. Model choice recorded per .claude/skills/dcf-methods/SKILL.md routing table (LIC / closed-end fund row) -- no prior DCF exists for MLN.NZ so this is a fresh build, not an update.

Marlin is a textbook case (Fisher Funds-managed, no debt, no SBC, formulaic NAV-based distribution) directly analogous to AFI.NZ and BIT.NZ already in this research folder, whose methodology this build follows exactly (headline IV = current NAV x scenario fair discount; 5yr IRR-build memo as cross-check; sanity check anchored to price/NAV history, not P/E). historical_growth.methodology: Marlin's own preferred value driver is NAV-per-share TOTAL RETURN (NAV growth + dividends paid, reinvested), disclosed in the annual report's 5-year performance table against the S&P Large Mid Cap/S&P Small Cap Index (50% hedged to NZ$) benchmark. Standard revenue/EPS/equity CAGRs are shown for schema completeness but are NOT the growth driver used in projections -- 'Revenue' and 'NetIncome' in the Metrics.csv are dominated by unrealised/realised capital gains timing (FY2021 NetIncome $69.2m vs FY2022 -$60.4m on a near-identical share count) rather than an operating trend.
historical_growth.growth_rate_source: nav_total_return_base_case_assumption (not a pure historical CAGR -- see notes)
historical_growth.growth_divergence_warning: Revenue/NetIncome/EPS CAGRs are not meaningful for this ticker and are left null rather than computed -- they are dominated by unrealised mark-to-market portfolio swings of the same order of magnitude as net assets (FY2021 NetIncome $69.2m on $244m equity vs FY2022 -$60.4m on $178m equity), not an operating growth trend. Equity (net assets) CAGR is similarly noisy: it reflects portfolio value swings, warrant exercise proceeds, and the DRP/buyback capital-management mix, not organic compounding -- do not use equity CAGR as the growth driver for this ticker.
historical_growth.notes: The defining historical fact for MLN.NZ is that NAV PER SHARE HAS BARELY MOVED in 8 years ($0.89 FY2017 -> $0.95 FY2025, a mere +0.82%/yr) despite a company-reported 5-year Adjusted NAV Return (total return including reinvested distributions) of +7.3% p.a. -- because the fixed 2%-of-average-NAV-per-quarter (~8%/yr) distribution policy persistently distributes essentially all of the portfolio's return, and often slightly more than NAV growth alone generates, keeping the per-share NAV roughly flat to mildly declining over a full cycle. The FY2025 result was the standout disappointment within that record: Gross Performance Return of only +2.7% badly lagged the +14.9% benchmark (a 12.2pp shortfall), driven by an overweight healthcare / zero-weight financials positioning the manager has since publicly acknowledged and moved to correct (six new positions added including Nvidia, Hermes, Costco, KKR; Dollar General/Dollar Tree exited). The base-case 7.0% total-return assumption sits just below the trailing 5yr Adjusted NAV Return (7.3%) and the 5yr Gross Performance Return (10.1%), reflecting a view that a modest persistent underperformance drag versus the benchmark (proven over 5 years at -2.8pp/yr, and far worse in FY2025 alone) continues but does not worsen further, net of the 1.25% fee and the FY2025 process changes only partially restoring relative performance.

base.rationale: Long-run global large-cap growth equity total return (~9-10%) net of Marlin's demonstrated 5-year benchmark underperformance (-2.8pp/yr, partially but not fully closed by the post-FY2025 process changes -- Fisher Funds has under 12 months' track record on the broadened, faster-turnover approach) and the ~1.25% management fee (partially offset by the underperformance-linked fee-floor rebate mechanism). The formulaic 8%/yr distribution policy then mechanically implies NAV per share DECLINES slightly (-1.0%/yr) at this total-return level, consistent with the observed 8-year plain-NAV-growth history of only +0.82%/yr. Exit discount of 8% sits between Marlin's FY2024/25 disclosed discount range (4.2%-5.8%) and the wider ~16% level reached in early/mid-August 2026, reflecting a view that today's unusually wide discount (driven by the FY2025 underperformance shock plus the FY2026 warrant-overhang commentary) partially but not fully normalises, since the buyback trigger (6% threshold) has not actually been used to defend the discount in H1 FY2026 despite being breached.

bull.rationale: The post-FY2025 portfolio review (broader sector/geography diversification, AI-exposed additions -- Nvidia, faster idea-generation cadence) succeeds in restoring gross performance toward or above the benchmark, cost of equity edges down on reduced perceived manager risk, and active use of the buyback/DRP capital-management tools (finally deployed at the 6% trigger, unlike H1 FY2026) closes the discount to par, consistent with the near-zero discount Marlin traded at as recently as 30-Jun-2026 per the Analysis JSON.

bear.rationale: Underperformance persists or worsens (the FY2025 shortfall was not a one-off but reflects a structural style-drift risk shared with sister funds Kingfish/Barramundi under the same STEEPP process), a global equity growth-stock drawdown hits the fully-invested, unleveraged, largely-unhedged portfolio (FY2022 precedent: -25.6% adjusted NAV return), the 57.3m-warrant overhang (~25% of shares) continues to be cited as discount-widening pressure into the April-2027 exercise date, and the board's buyback trigger continues to go unused as observed in H1 FY2026 -- holding the discount at the ~16% wide reached in mid-August 2026 rather than reverting.

five_year_irr_build_memo.description: Cross-check to the headline 'current NAV x fair discount' intrinsic value: PV of the 5-year dividend stream plus PV of the year-5 exit value (year-5 NAV x scenario exit discount), both discounted at the scenario's cost of equity. This captures compounding of NAV growth (and its slow decline under the distribution formula) over the horizon that the simpler current-NAV framing does not.

base.terminal_pct_of_value: n/a -- not an FCF DCF; see five_year_irr_build_memo (exit value is ~65% of the 5yr-build fair value)
base.implied_exit_multiple: n/a -- LIC valuation uses P/NAV, not an earnings multiple

entry_price.methodology: Price today such that 5 years of projected base-case dividends plus the year-5 exit value (year-5 NAV x base-case 8% exit discount) discounted at 15% equals that price. Uses base-case cashflows only, per dcf-analyst methodology, and the post-2026-07-21 formula (interim cashflows + terminal value at the hurdle rate, not terminal value alone).
entry_price.memo: A 15% IRR hurdle applied to an asset whose base-case total return is only ~7% p.a. (and whose distribution formula mechanically erodes NAV per share over time) requires buying at a very deep discount to today's NAV (~-30% implied P/NAV at entry, versus Marlin's own disclosed historical discount range of roughly -30.5% (FY2021 PREMIUM) to +16% (Aug-2026 wide)). This entry price sits near the deepest discount Marlin has shown on the discount side of its range (excluding the FY2021/22 premium era, which reflected a growth-stock bubble, not a repeatable valuation regime), so it is a plausible but aggressive target rather than an achievable near-term certainty. A diversified, unleveraged global-growth-equity LIC with a ~7-9% expected total return should more realistically be judged against its cost of equity (~9.5%), not a 15% private-equity-style hurdle -- on that basis, buying today at NZ$0.779 (an ~8.9% discount to the latest $0.8547 NAV) offers a prospective return close to the base-case ~7% total return, since the current discount already sits within (not beyond) the base-case assumed 8% fair discount.

sanity_check.description: For a closed-end LIC the natural sanity anchor is price/NAV (P/NAV), not P/E or EV/EBITDA -- both set to null below because reported NetIncome is dominated by unrealised mark-to-market portfolio swings of the same order of magnitude as net assets (e.g. FY2021 +$69.2m vs FY2022 -$60.4m) and there is no EBITDA concept for a portfolio of listed securities. The check trips if a scenario's implied P/NAV sits outside Marlin's own disclosed historical price/NAV range; none of the three scenarios below breach that range (base -8.0%, bull 0.0%, bear -16.0%, all within the -30.5% premium to (at least) -16% discount extremes actually observed), so the check passes.

implied_multiples.price_to_earnings: n/a -- NetIncome is mark-to-market, not an operating earnings concept
implied_multiples.ev_to_ebitda: n/a -- no EBITDA concept for a listed-securities portfolio

sanity_check.historical_pnav_range_note: FY2021 (-30.5%, i.e. a 30.5% PREMIUM) and FY2022 (-25.8% premium) reflect the post-COVID growth-stock bubble and should not be treated as a recurring regime -- the more relevant recent range is FY2023-FY2025's 1.1% to 5.8% DISCOUNT, widening sharply through 2026 to ~9% (14-Jul), ~14% (31-Jul) and ~16% (11-Aug), before narrowing back to ~8.9% at the current live price against the latest disclosed NAV.
sanity_check.note: Current market price (-8.9% to the latest $0.8547 NAV) sits almost exactly at the base-case assumed fair discount (-8.0%), meaning the base-case scenario is essentially pricing where the market already trades -- the small +0.94% base-case upside reflects this near-equilibrium read rather than a clear mispricing signal in either direction. The bear case (-16%) matches the widest discount actually observed in the FY2026 trading history (11-Aug-2026), and the bull case (0%, par) matches the near-parity level Marlin briefly traded at as recently as 30-Jun-2026 -- both scenario bookends are therefore anchored to real, recently observed trading levels rather than theoretical extremes.

sensitivity.methodology: 5-year IRR-build fair value (PV of dividends + PV of exit value at year-5 NAV x row exit discount, both discounted at the 9.5% base-case cost of equity) in NZD.

probability_weighted.weights_rationale: House default 25/50/25 (not the 15/50/35 operating-company default, which is calibrated to solvency/refinancing risk that does not apply to an unleveraged LIC). Bear is not overweighted beyond the default because MLN carries zero debt and the downside case is a discount/market-return outcome, not a going-concern risk.
